say.text: A 62-year-old has a firm, painless lump in one breast. Her team plans chemotherapy before any operation, so they need a tissue sample the pathologist can report on. Which sample do you send?

choices.label: Fine needle aspiration cytology of the lump
Core needle biopsy of the lump, read by histology
Excision of the whole lump, sent for histology
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Right. Core needle biopsy is the investigation of choice for tissue diagnosis, and it is the sample to send before treatment starts.

choices.label: Next

say.text: That is not the right choice.
Fine needle aspiration is the old exam key for breast lumps and it is quick. Core biopsy is the preferred tissue test, because it gives a histology sample rather than loose cells.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so slow down: check what the pathologist must be able to report before you pick the method.

choices.label: Try again

say.text: That is not the right choice.
Excision is a surgical step. Tissue for the decision has to come first, before any operation is planned.

choices.label: Try again

say.text: Ask which test gives the pathologist a tissue sample to report on, without cutting the whole lump out first.

choices.label: Back to the question

say.text: Your registrar says, 'Every new lump gets a mammogram first, it is the screening test.' A 29-year-old has a new breast lump. What is the right first imaging?

choices.label: Breast ultrasound, the first test for her lump
MRI of both breasts, to see the whole picture
Mammogram, as the registrar says, for her lump
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Right. Under 35, ultrasound is the imaging of choice for a breast lump.

choices.label: Next

say.text: That is not the right choice.
MRI is used to define extent or solve a problem, not as the first test for a lump in a young woman.

choices.label: Try again

say.text: That is not the right choice.
The registrar's rule ignores age. Under 35 the imaging of choice differs, so age is the qualifier to check first.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so check the age qualifier in the stem before you accept any blanket rule.

choices.label: Try again

say.text: Look at the age in the stem. Does the registrar's rule account for it?

choices.label: Back to the question

say.text: A classmate writes: 'Bone is the commonest site of spread, so every new breast cancer gets a bone scan.' Which correction is right?

choices.label: Agree: scan every case, since bone is where spread goes
Agree, but scan after surgery rather than before
Scans are for advanced disease or symptoms; early cancer skips them
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Right. Bone is the commonest site of distant spread, but scans are for locally advanced disease or symptoms, not every case.

choices.label: Next

say.text: That is not the right choice.
The classmate has moved from where spread lands to who gets tested. Bone being the commonest site does not make a scan routine for every patient.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so test the step from 'where spread goes' to 'who needs a scan'.

choices.label: Try again

say.text: That is not the right choice.
A scan after surgery still does not answer whether she needs imaging at all. The indication depends on stage and symptoms.

choices.label: Try again

say.text: Ask what a scan is for. In which patients does it find something that changes the plan?

choices.label: Back to the question

say.text: Which of these is a relative factor that weighs against breast conservation, rather than a fixed rule?

choices.label: Multicentric disease in two separate quadrants of one breast
A tumour large for its breast, leaving poor cosmesis
Any tumour above 5 cm, whatever the size of the breast
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Right. Size is judged against the breast, and a large tumour in a small breast leaves poor cosmesis, so it weighs against conservation.

choices.label: Next

say.text: That is not the right choice.
Multicentric disease is a fixed bar to conservation, not a relative factor, so it does not fit what the question asks.

choices.label: Try again

say.text: That is not the right choice.
A fixed 5 cm cut-off looks like a rule, but conservation depends on tumour size against breast size, so a number alone does not settle it.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so ask whether the factor is fixed or depends on the breast it sits in.

choices.label: Try again

say.text: Ask whether the factor is a fixed rule, or whether it depends on how big the tumour is for the breast.

choices.label: Back to the question

say.text: A 46-year-old has a 1.6 cm invasive cancer. Her axilla feels normal on examination. Which order of axillary steps is right?

choices.label: Sentinel node biopsy first, then clearance if that node is positive
Clear levels I and II first; sentinel biopsy if clearance fails
Axillary radiotherapy alone, with no sampling first

say.text: Right. The sentinel node tells you whether the axilla needs clearing, so clearance follows only when that node is positive.

choices.label: Next

say.text: That is not the right choice.
Clearing the axilla first was the classical order, and it still tempts. But it dissects an axilla that only needed staging.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so check what the axilla needs to know before you choose an operation.

choices.label: Try again

say.text: That is not the right choice.
Radiotherapy does not stage the axilla. A sample is needed to decide what the axilla needs next.

choices.label: Try again

say.text: Which statement about nerve injury after axillary clearance is right?

choices.label: Numbness is the usual deficit, from the intercostobrachial nerve
Winging is the usual deficit, from the long thoracic nerve
Weak abduction is the usual deficit, from the thoracodorsal nerve

say.text: Right. The intercostobrachial nerve is the one most often sacrificed, and its injury gives numbness of the medial arm.

choices.label: Next

say.text: That is not the right choice.
Winging is the dramatic deficit, so it feels like the common one. It comes from the long thoracic nerve, which is injured less often than the intercostobrachial.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so separate how dramatic a deficit is from how often it occurs.

choices.label: Try again

say.text: That is not the right choice.
Thoracodorsal injury weakens latissimus dorsi. It is a real deficit, but not the one clearance most often causes.

choices.label: Try again

say.text: A classmate says: 'Tamoxifen is an anti-oestrogen, so it thins the endometrium and protects the uterus.' Which correction is right?

choices.label: Agree: it protects the uterus, so no endometrial checks are needed
Tamoxifen can raise endometrial cancer risk, so bleeding needs checking
The real danger is thrombosis, not uterine cancer

say.text: Right. Tamoxifen raises endometrial cancer risk, and thromboembolism is another serious effect. Raloxifene does not carry the endometrial risk.

choices.label: Next

say.text: That is not the right choice.
Blocking oestrogen in breast tissue does not carry over to the uterus, where tamoxifen can raise endometrial cancer risk.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so check whether the breast effect is the same as the uterine effect.

choices.label: Try again

say.text: That is not the right choice.
Thrombosis is a real side effect, but the uterine risk is the one this correction has to keep.

choices.label: Try again

say.text: You are writing the one-line take-home for stage III breast cancer with fixed axillary nodes and no distant spread. Which line is the best summary?

choices.label: Radiotherapy first to shrink the tumour, then surgery
Chemotherapy first to downstage, then surgery, then radiotherapy
Operate first to remove the bulk, then chemotherapy and radiotherapy

say.text: Right. In locally advanced disease, neoadjuvant chemotherapy comes first to downstage it, then surgery, then radiotherapy.

choices.label: Next

say.text: That is not the right choice.
Radiotherapy is a local treatment. It does not downstage fixed nodes or treat spread, so it cannot lead the plan.

choices.label: Try again

say.text: That is not the right choice.
Removing the bulk feels like the curative step, but fixed nodes mean spread may already exist beyond the breast, and surgery cannot reach it.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so ask what the first treatment must reach before the operation.

choices.label: Try again

say.text: Which of these is a recognised risk factor for breast cancer in men?

choices.label: Early menarche, a long reproductive lifespan
Klinefelter syndrome, a chromosomal condition in men
BRCA1 mutation, the gene most linked to men

say.text: Right. Klinefelter syndrome is a male risk factor, and BRCA2 is the gene more associated with male breast cancer.

choices.label: Next

say.text: That is not the right choice.
Early menarche is a risk factor for women through longer oestrogen exposure. It is not a recognised factor for men.

choices.label: Try again

say.text: That is not the right choice.
BRCA1 is the best-known breast gene, so it feels right for every hereditary question. The male-linked factor is a different one, so check which phenotype the stem describes.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so check which risk factor the stem's phenotype points to, not the best-known gene.

choices.label: Try again

cards.q: Which tissue test for a breast lump, and why not FNAC?
cards.a: Core needle biopsy, the investigation of choice; FNAC is the old key. Under 35, ultrasound is the imaging.

cards.q: When are distant-spread scans done in breast cancer?
cards.a: For locally advanced disease or symptoms, not routinely in early asymptomatic cancer. Bone is the commonest distant site.

cards.q: Which operation for operable breast cancer, and how do Halsted and MRM differ?
cards.a: Breast conservation with radiotherapy when suitable, or MRM. Halsted removes pectoralis major and minor; MRM keeps pectoralis major.

cards.q: First axillary step for a clinically node-negative patient?
cards.a: Sentinel lymph node biopsy; clear the axilla if the sentinel node is positive.

cards.q: First treatment for stage III or inflammatory breast cancer?
cards.a: Neoadjuvant chemotherapy to downstage, then surgery, then radiotherapy.

cards.q: Hormone drug by menopausal status, and tamoxifen's endometrial effect?
cards.a: Tamoxifen premenopausal; aromatase inhibitor postmenopausal. Tamoxifen raises endometrial cancer risk.

cards.q: Which nerve is most often injured in axillary clearance, and what does long thoracic injury cause?
cards.a: Intercostobrachial, giving numbness of the medial arm; long thoracic injury gives winging of the scapula.
